text: When below the east face, scramble up through brush and easy rock to an obvious slabby rock face just left of the small pocket glacier on the east face.
runs: an obvious slabby rock face just left of the small pocket glacier on the east face

text: Follows the standard approach to Headlee Pass, then crosses the talus toward Lake Elan/Vesper Lake and takes the first ramp up and right to the base of the South Ridge. The route climbs the ridgecrest with a brief detour onto its left side about halfway up: a ~200 ft, Class 4 first tower, then easier Class 2-3 climbing back to the ridgecrest, a 5th-class section (which is actually a downclimb off a block), then a couple more ropelengths of Class 3-4 to a false summit, and a couple more ropelengths beyond that to the true summit. Simul-climbing or moving unroped is recommended rather than pitching it out formally.

text: Approach to Headlee Pass as for the standard route (see that route's approach). Cross the talus toward Vesper/Elan Lake, then take the first ramp heading up and to the right to reach the base of the South Ridge.
runs: lake then take the first ramp heading up and to the right

text: From the summit, follow the standard Class 3 route down to the west to the pass between Vesper and Sperry, then head south back over Headlee Pass and down to the car - do not try to reverse the South Ridge itself.
runs: down to the west to the pass between vesper and sperry then head south back

text: One feature settles this: a prominent rock buttress bisects the peak's south face, and the gully you want is the one immediately to its right, to the east. Get there by dropping off the south side of the col — slither down the shallow moat beside the steep snow finger rather than fighting the snow itself — then traverse eastward across a broad slope of dirt, scree and talus cut by erosion runnels, angling up toward the face. The proof at the gully's foot is a deep, ugly erosion runnel spewing out of its mouth. Rather than crossing that runnel head-on, take the talus ramp beside it that leads up and into the gully. Inside, the gully is very narrow, quite steep and completely choked with loose rock: if the gully you are in is broad, clean or comfortable, it is the wrong one. If the big central buttress is on your right rather than your left, you have gone one gully too far west.
runs: eastward across a broad slope of dirt scree and talus

text: Gap on the divide between the east and west drainage basins; gain Spinnaker's south ridge here and angle climber's-left up the final slopes to the summit.
runs: divide between the east and west drainage basins

text: Spire Mountain (6,213-6,218 ft) is a three-summited peak — Northwest, Central, and Southeast Spires — in the Wild Sky Wilderness of the Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, about 7 miles northeast of Index and 4 miles north-northeast of Gunn Peak. It rises directly above the North Fork Skykomish River, on the west side of the range, not near Sultan Basin or the Sauk drainage/Monte Cristo group. One of the least-often-climbed of the 'Everett Pin Peaks,' Spire is reached by a long, entirely off-trail approach through brush and cliff bands and finishes on an airy summit ridge with a genuine, exposed Class 5 step that trips up parties expecting an easy Class 3 walk-up.
runs: one of the least often climbed of the everett pin peaks

text: Leave the road on the side away from the river and climb steeply, off-trail, through downed timber; the first 600 ft are steep but brush-free. After crossing an old logging road, traverse obliquely left to a saddle at about 2,300 ft, where you cross a second old overgrown logging road.
runs: steep but brush free after crossing an old logging road

text: Hike north up Itswoot Ridge, staying on talus on its west side near the stream to bypass the rock towers directly above camp; the crest itself is only walkable in short gentle stretches. Snow is usually continuous above about 6,800 ft, so crampons and an axe come out here. You can either climb the moderate 30-degree snow straight to the col or skirt the left edge of the snowfield on rock.
runs: you can either climb the moderate 30 degree snow

text: Summit is tiny — room for only one person at a time
runs: room for only one person at a time

text: Short, excellent leaning crack on the left that starts at #3 size and gets smaller, the trickiest section of the route; only two or three pieces. The easier option is the blocky trough and gully to its right: walk a short ledge to an exposed step, then climb a second steep groove.
runs: right walk a short ledge to an exposed step

text:
The marker at the base is dead trees. As the ground steepens toward the formation and before the gully, look on your left for tree snags — standing dead timber against the rock. The first pitch climbs cracks up from a snag. That is the start, and it is the only start on this formation with a landmark you can walk up and touch.

If you have entered the gully itself, you have gone too far right. The gully parallels this route and is used both as a descent and as a fast way to reach the bolted line beside it — it is not this climb.

Confirm on pitch two, which is the strongest check the route gives you: it traverses under a roof. If your second pitch runs sideways beneath an overhang rather than straight up, you are on line. Above that expect steepening ground with cracks and a good layback, then a wide ten-inch crack with finger and hand sections, then a corner crack to lieback, and a headwall finish.

Expect long scrambling sections between the pitches. That is this route's defining character and the main complaint about it — it is the reason a 5.7 with seven pitches takes a full day. Continuous roped climbing with no walking between would mean you are somewhere else.

Negative markers for the two neighbours. If you have traversed a long way rightward from the base on third and fourth-class ledges toward the middle of the face before starting, you are heading for the hard line that finishes on this route's last pitches. And if your first pitch is protected by bolts, you are on the partly bolted line — this route takes natural gear throughout.

Descent is most often a rappel of the line itself, and parties report it is slow and that ropes snag on flakes. The alternative is the third-class gully to climbers' right, faster but loose; stay high and skier's-right to limit what is above you.
runs: before the gully look on your left for

text:
Park in the highway turnout about two miles east of Washington Pass, near milepost 165. The climbers' trail starts at the far west end of the pullout, drops steeply through loose dirt and rock, crosses Early Winters Creek on logs, then traverses an avalanche path — the old line has two or three informal fixed rope sections here — toward the base of the formation. Around an hour and a half.

A newer variation of the path bears right just before the fixed lines and needs only a small amount of scrambling, which most parties now prefer.

There are two ways to reach this route once you are under the formation, and they are genuinely different days. The faster one takes the gully that parallels the arete beside it. The other climbs the first three pitches of that arete and then cuts across the gully, which is how parties who wanted a longer outing get here.
runs: at the far west end of the pullout

text: A section of pitch 1 (and at least one of its bolts) collapsed in a 2013 rockfall, so don't count on the original bolt count matching older topos
runs: at least one of its bolts collapsed in

text: Traverse right another 25' to a short finger crack in the corner and build an anchor.
runs: traverse right another 25 to a short finger crack in the corner and build an anchor

text: Drop the overnight pack and go light: up the scree bowl south of the lake to the pass, contour around point 7912, then follow the SW ridge east to the summit. It's technically easy…
runs: bowl south of the lake to the pass

text: Drop the overnight pack and go light: up the scree bowl south of the lake to the pass, contour around point 7912, then follow the SW ridge east to the summit. It's technically easy but slow, loose scree/talus travel with some easy hands-and-feet scrambling near the top. Strong parties often tag Courtney and/or Oval Peak from the same camp, but this plan covers Star Peak alone.
runs: bowl south of the lake to the pass

text: Start about 50 ft left of Good Girls Like Bad Boys at a two-bolt stance on a narrow part of Madsen's Ledge (a hand line has been in place). Face and arete past three bolts reach a steep corner with a crack in the back; stem and jam it on cams, then a tricky arete and more stemming lead to a semi-hanging belay.

a steep corner with a crack in the back stem and

text: Descent reverses the ascent line. From the notch/crack area just below the true summit, most parties downclimb the ~15-ft crux crack and the exposed Class 4 ledge just below it. Some instead rappel off the fixed slings (in-situ tat/webbing — inspect it and back it up before committing) back to the ledge on the north side; even with a 60 m rope, expect to downclimb some Class 3 terrain. From the ledge, cross back through the right-most notch and descend the loose talus and scree slope to the cirque. From the base of the talus, traverse back to the basin below Goode and descend the cairned climbers' path and the burned ridge to the Park Creek trail just past the big washout, then continue via whichever of the three approach trails (Thunder Creek, McAlester Pass/Rainbow Creek, or Park Creek/Stehekin) matches your itinerary. Loose rock is the dominant descent hazard from the summit all the way down through the talus — keep helmets on and parties tight until well below the scree.
runs: back to the ledge on the north side even with a 60 m rope

text: Continue up the Park Creek Pass Trail about 2 miles, then leave the trail around 4,100 ft at a large washout and climb diagonally climber's-left through heather, meadows and game trails. Terrain steepens and turns rocky near 6,500 ft; cairns then mark a Class 2-3 climber's trail up to the basin below Goode at 7,400 ft, a strenuous full day with an overnight pack. This basin (or the rib just south of it) is the standard high camp for both Storm King and Goode.
runs: mark a class 2 3 climber's trail up to

text: Optional: most parties downclimb the crux crack and the exposed Class 4 ledge instead. The rappel goes off the east side back to the ledge on the north side; even with a 60 m rope, expect to downclimb some Class 3 terrain after it.
runs: back to the ledge on the north side even with a 60 m rope

text: Flat, grassy camp on a small NE/SW-trending rib just south of Storm King, with a nearby water source. It is reached by a mostly level traverse from the basin below Goode.
runs: small ne/sw trending rib just south of storm king

text: Walk down the highway toward Mazama to where the climbers' track leaves the road. Below the initial scree slope a user trail leads to the log crossing of Early Winters Creek (careful on the logs). From there pick your own way up through the boulder field to the base of the wall, about 20 to 30 minutes in all.
runs: up through the boulder field to the base of the wall about 20

text: A rarely repeated, sustained alpine ice line up a series of runnels and couloirs just right of the true summit on Summit Chief's north side, with unusually continuous ice climbing for a Cascade route.
runs: series of runnels and couloirs just right of the

text: The line is the chain of runnels and couloirs just right of the true summit on the north face. Start up the avalanche cone at the foot of the face, then climb neve on the lower face into the ramp.
runs: of runnels and couloirs just right of the

text: Follow the Pete Lake Trail #1323 up the Cooper River on gentle, mostly flat forest tread about 4.5 miles to Pete Lake, then continue to a fork about five miles in and turn right. After about 0.6 mile, turn right again onto the Pacific Crest Trail.
runs: turn right again onto the pacific crest trail

text:
Walk the Pete Lake trail #1323 up the Cooper River to a fork at about 3,120 ft, roughly five miles in. Turn right, continue about six tenths of a mile, and turn right again onto the Pacific Crest Trail at about 3,220 ft. Follow the PCT four and a half miles up a long series of switchbacks to about 5,500 ft.

The Vista Lakes tarns lie east of the trail at that height and hold the good bivy sites. Summit Chief is about two more miles from there. Reported times from the car to the upper lake run to most of a day with overnight loads, and every published account treats this as a two- or three-day trip.

This is also the last reliable water. The ground above is reported bone dry until you come back down to the lakes.

From camp, leave the PCT and traverse cross-country toward Summit Chief Pass, then follow the ridge north-west staying below the cliffs and gendarmes, into the upper basin south-east of the main summit. One party's hindsight on this traverse is worth having: they should have dropped to about 6,000 ft and taken the scree instead of holding height across steep sloping slabs.
runs: turn right again onto the pacific crest trail

text:
There is a specific chain of features here and it ends at a piece of ground that is unmistakable once you know to look for it.

From the upper basin, find a small notch in the skyline ridge to the west. To reach it, head north-west toward a minor rock ridge that runs west-south-west to east-north-east across the base of the summit. That minor ridge is the base of the climb — arriving at it is arriving.

Gain it by the snow in the gap at its right, lower end, then walk along the top of the ridge to the notch at its west end. On the far side of the notch is a steep gully, usually icy in the morning, and beyond that a loose-rock gully; the exit is the gully on the right just below the summit.

Negative marker, learned the hard way and independently corroborated: from the snowfield below the south-east face, the first and left-most snow finger leading to the south ridge is a dead end. It runs into a deep notch and the party that took it had to retreat. Go instead to the upper right corner of the snowfield, exit onto steep dirt and scree, and pick up a left-slanting ramp to a higher notch. Two separate accounts arrive at the same instruction from opposite directions.

The moat is the gate and it has a date on it. Where the mountain rises in earnest at about 7,000 ft a moat forms, and it may be impassable after mid-July, perhaps earlier in a low-snow year. If it stops you, there may be Class 3 rock in the middle of the basin as an alternative, but plan the trip around the calendar rather than hoping.

Do not trust a single photograph for the crossing point on the south ridge; parties report the pictures circulating online do not match the ground.

The top five hundred feet is steep dirt and thoroughly untrustworthy rock — one climber said it had earned honorary Olympic Mountains status. That looseness is normal for this summit and is not a sign you have wandered onto harder ground.

side of the notch is a steep gully

text: Starts with an approach pitch of rambly ice leading to a solid ~25 ft near-vertical curtain (WI4), continues up nearly 60m of solid fat WI3 ice in the main gully, eases through 100+m of easier terrain with ice smears through an easy chimney, then finishes with a short WI3 step before the upper snowfields.
runs: to a solid 25 ft near vertical curtain

text: 6-8 ice screws, optionally a few light rock pieces and a picket.
runs: optionally a few light rock pieces and a picket

text: From the Lower Curtis Glacier, about 600 ft of steep snow in the lower icefall (45 degrees at the top) leads to a large transverse crevasse (crossed on a snow bridge), then a short band of vertical ice in a rock chimney, about 150 ft more steep snow to the top of the icefall, and 60 ft of unprotected 5.0 rock onto the glacier tongue. 100 ft of steep snow leads to a second large transverse crevasse (crossed on the left), then 300 ft of steep ice/snow (60 degrees at the bottom, 70 near the top) to the headwall base. Traverse left at the headwall to a weakness with 100 ft of 4th class to a ledge, traverse left around a corner, then climb ~1,000 ft of easy 5th-class rock on good rock to the crest of the main SE Ridge.
runs: steep snow to the top of the icefall
to the crest of the main se ridge

text: Above the chimney, climb steep snow to the top of the icefall and an unprotected band of easy fifth-class rock onto the glacier tongue, cross the second crevasse at its left end, and climb 60 to 70 degree ice to the headwall. Traverse left on fourth-class rock and around a corner to the long buttress, follow it to the Southeast Ridge, then drop east onto the Sulphide Glacier and go north to climb the summit pyramid.
runs: steep snow to the top of the icefall

text: Approach from Lake Ann; from below the Fisher Chimneys, traverse right (east) onto the Lower Curtis Glacier and follow it to the upper SE corner of the glacier basin below the couloir.
runs: approach from lake ann from below the fisher
traverse right east onto the lower curtis glacier and

text: Start from the upper SE corner of the Lower Curtis Glacier, on the snow slope below the obvious glacier tongue that reaches halfway up the face, aiming for the narrow gully at the right side of the main wall. The slope steepens to about 45° near its top and ends at a large transverse crevasse, crossed on a snow bridge; check the bridge before committing.
runs: from the upper se corner of the lower curtis glacier

text: At the base of the headwall traverse left to a less-than-vertical weakness and climb it on fourth-class rock to a ledge. From the ledge traverse left around a corner to reach the foot of the long buttress.
runs: headwall traverse left to a less than vertical weakness

text: A long buttress of easy fifth-class climbing on good, solid rock with positive holds, climbed for roughly its whole height to the crest of the main SE Ridge south of the Hourglass. A minimal rack of nuts and extra-long slings covers it.
runs: to the crest of the main se ridge south of the hourglass

text: Drop off the east side of the rocky SE Ridge crest onto the Sulphide Glacier and follow it north to the south side of the summit pyramid. Rope up for the glacier; it is crevassed.
runs: north to the south side of the summit pyramid

text: Climb the summit pyramid by the regular fourth-class line, or take a direct line of roughly 800 ft of easy fifth-class rock. In low visibility on the way down, stay high and traverse directly below the Hourglass to avoid the Upper Curtis icefall.
runs: stay high and traverse directly below the hourglass

text:
From the Lake Ann Trailhead on SR-542, about a mile below Artist Point at roughly 4,770 ft, take Lake Ann Trail #600 to the lake and on toward the Fisher Chimneys.

Before the Chimneys, traverse right — east — onto the Lower Curtis Glacier and follow it up to the upper southeast corner of the glacier basin. This is where the technical climbing starts, at the foot of the icefall.

The descent for this route goes back via the Hourglass and the Upper Curtis to the Shuksan Arm — the Fisher Chimneys descent — so the day is a loop rather than a reverse, and the whole thing is commonly cited at around eight hours round trip from Lake Ann.
runs: traverse right east onto the lower curtis glacier and

text: The classic SW ridge of the highest peak in the range: the route begins with loose, blocky climbing low down, then the final two pitches offer delightful easy climbing on cracks and knobs along an exposed ridge to the summit. All routes in the Gunsight Range are short, and this one runs about 5 pitches.
runs: the classic sw ridge of the highest peak in the range the

text: 2 double-rope rappels: one from near the summit to the notch between Middle and South Gunsight, one more into the moat at the base of the notch. With only one 60 m rope expect more; no single-rope count is published.

the moat at the base of the notch

text: Follow the Pacific Crest Trail and Agnes Creek trail about 9 to 10 miles, cross Agnes Creek on a log, and bushwhack steeply about 5,000 ft into the upper Blue Glacier basin to a high camp on the rock ridge above the glacier, below the east side of the Gunsight peaks. From camp, work around to the west side of the towers and climb the Southwest Ridge to the summit.
runs: around to the west side of the towers and

text: From the summit, traverse south along the summit ridge to the south-facing rappel anchors and make two double-rope rappels: the first to the notch between Middle and South Gunsight, the second into the moat at the base of the notch (loose, dirty and cold). With a single 60 m rope expect more rappels. From the glacier, reverse the approach: descend roughly 5,000 ft back to Agnes Creek and hike out 9-10 miles to High Bridge.
runs: the moat at the base of the notch

text: From Twisp, take SR 20 east about 2 miles and continue south on SR 153 about 12 miles, then turn right onto Gold Creek Loop Road and follow it to Gold Creek Road. Drive Gold Creek Road about 5 miles, turn left onto Forest Road 4340-200, and follow it about 3.6 miles to the Foggy Dew Trailhead at road's end, about 3,400 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required to park.

text: From the Artist Point trailhead (elev. ~5,100 ft, at the end of Mt. Baker Highway/SR 542, GPS approx. 48.847, -121.693) walk to the northwest corner of the large paved parking lot — the signed Table Mountain Trail #681 starts opposite the vault toilets, on the side of the lot away from the highway. The trail begins as a rock-lined gravel path that climbs gently before reaching its first switchback within a few hundred feet. From there the route ascends a tight set of rocky switchbacks blasted directly into the cliff band on Table Mountain's southeast face — this is the crux of the approach: a narrow, exposed catwalk with steep drop-offs toward the Chain Lakes basin and Swift Creek drainage 400-800 ft below. Footing here is loose rock and gravel over hard-packed tread, and snow or verglas frequently lingers in this cliff section into July, making it the most hazardous stretch of the whole route; many parties turn back here in early season without traction devices. After roughly 400 ft of gain (about 0.4-0.5 mi from the car) the switchbacks top out on the broad, relatively flat summit plateau ("the table"). From here follow the well-trodden tread west/northwest along the south rim, which gives open views straight down onto the Chain Lakes Trail; numerous braided use-trails cross the plateau but the main route hugs the south side. At about 1.2 mi you reach the east side of the tabletop with views of Mount Baker and Ptarmigan Ridge, and by 1.3 mi you arrive at two small tarns that frame Mount Shuksan — a natural turnaround for most day hikers and the last easily identified landmark before the trail degrades into a sketchy, unmaintained scramble path descending toward the Table Mountain Glacier. There is no reliable water along the route: the summit tarns are shallow, silty, and not worth treating, so carry all water from the car. Overall to the high point is roughly 1.4-1.5 mi one-way with about 700-725 ft of gain from the trailhead.
runs: the trail begins as a rock lined gravel path

text:
From the Artist Point trailhead at about 5,100 ft, at the end of the Mount Baker Highway, walk to the northwest corner of the large paved parking lot. Table Mountain Trail #681 starts opposite the vault toilets, on the side of the lot away from the highway.

The trail begins as a rock-lined gravel path and reaches its first switchback within a few hundred feet. From there it climbs a tight set of rocky switchbacks blasted directly into the cliff band on Table Mountain's southeast face — a narrow, exposed catwalk with drops of 400-800 ft toward the Chain Lakes basin and Swift Creek.

After roughly 400 ft of gain, about 0.4-0.5 mile from the car, the switchbacks top out on the broad flat summit plateau. Follow the tread west-northwest along the south rim; braided use-trails cross the plateau but the main route hugs the south side. At about 1.3 miles two small tarns frame Mount Shuksan and mark the usual turnaround.

There is no water: the tarns are shallow and silty. Carry everything from the car.
runs: the trail begins as a rock lined gravel path and

text: Drive US-2 east from Monroe to Baring. At milepost 41, across from the store, turn left onto 635th Place NE, cross the railroad tracks, go 0.3 mile and keep left at the junction. The road becomes FR 6024 (Barclay Creek Road); follow it 3.9 potholed miles to the road-end trailhead at about 2,300 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass is required.

text: From Monroe, drive US-2 east to Baring; near milepost 41, opposite a convenience store, turn left (north) onto 635th Place NE, cross the railroad tracks, continue 0.3 mi, keep left at the junction for another 0.1 mi as the road becomes FR-6024, then continue 3.9 miles (watch for potholes) to the Barclay Lake Trailhead.

text: The striking black-and-white streaked open corner right of Swim and Green Dragon, almost directly above where the trail reaches the wall. Tricky steep moves low in the corner lead into pumpy overhanging climbing on sloping edges and pockets; the hardest section is short, then angle and difficulty ease toward the ledge anchor. Often wet from the waterfall until summer.
runs: pumpy overhanging climbing on sloping edges and pockets

text: From Thunder Basin at 5,180 feet, ascend snowfields and rocky slopes toward the summit block. The final two pitches involve Class 4 scrambling up a gully left of the summit col (approximately 85 feet to a ledge), followed by a longer pitch up a face toward a broken chimney containing a good jam crack that leads directly to the summit. Crampons and ice axe essential for snowfield sections. A fixed pin exists for rappel descent assistance. The route sees minimal traffic and requires solid route-finding skills.
runs: pitch up a face toward a broken chimney

text: Alpine start up snow/talus to the col east of the summit block, then a loose gully and a broken, jam-crack chimney (class 4/easy 5th) to the top. Most parties rappel the chimney/fa…
runs: to the col east of the summit block

text: Alpine start up snow/talus to the col east of the summit block, then a loose gully and a broken, jam-crack chimney (class 4/easy 5th) to the top. Most parties rappel the chimney/face on descent rather than downclimbing since there are no fixed anchors — carry gear to build rap stations and leave slung horns/webbing.
runs: to the col east of the summit block

text:
The col east of the summit block is the base, and the thing that confirms it is the wind. Parties who have stood there describe it as an incredibly windy notch below the east face — it is a gap on a ridge, so it funnels, and on a Cascade summit day you will feel it before you can see anything.

Getting there is a single bearing from camp: from Thunder Basin cross talus and snow toward the col that sits east of the summit block, near 8,000 ft. Crampons and an axe are normal for the snow, which stays firm in the morning. You are aiming for the gap beside the summit tower, not for the tower.

The positive test for the start of the climbing: from the col the route takes a loose gully on the left for about 85 ft to a ledge system. Loose first, ledge second. If the first thing above the col is clean solid rock, or if you are moving right rather than left, you are not on it.

The second confirmation is a crack. Above the ledge system the finish is a broken chimney with a good jam crack running up it, and that crack is the one genuinely positive hold-bearing feature on the summit block. Class 4 to easy fifth depending on conditions. If you are on a face with no chimney and no crack, you have drifted off the ledge system.

What it is not: this is a short summit block, not a wall. From the col to the top is roughly two rope lengths. If you have been climbing for hours above the col you are not on this route.

Rack and rock: everything from the col up is loose. Helmet, and space the party out — the gully drops what the leader pulls straight onto whoever is below.
runs: a broken chimney with a good jam crack

text: Talus and snow to the col east of the summit block
runs: to the col east of the summit block

text: From the Lena Lake Trailhead (Trail #810) off FS-25 at roughly 700 ft, hike the maintained Lena Lake Trail about 3 miles and ~1,100 ft of gain through second-growth and old-growth forest, crossing several creek drainages on the way, to Lena Lake (~1,800 ft) — a popular backpacking destination with a ranger station and established campsites, and the last easy, reliable water/camping before the climbers' route. Skirt the west side of the lake and pick up the unmaintained but well-trodden 'Brothers Trail' boot path, which continues up the East Fork Lena Creek drainage through the old-growth 'Valley of the Silent Men' for roughly another 2.5-3 miles to a climbers' camp (sometimes called Camp Brothers) at about 2,900 ft, marked by a fire ring — most parties treat this as their high camp for a two-day ascent. From camp, leave the tread and follow a climbers' path along the west fork of Lena Creek for about a mile; this crosses an avalanche debris field where slide alder and downed logs (some with hand-lines/notches cut in) obscure the route and creek fords may be required — go carefully, especially with a full pack. Beyond the debris field the path re-enters forest and climbs to the base of the South Couloir around 4,000-4,300 ft. Ascend the couloir (firm snow in early season, loose scree by mid/late summer) a few hundred feet, then exit onto its west side and continue up scree to about 5,000 ft, making an ascending rightward traverse below cliff bands to reach the crest of a semi-open spur. From the spur, work up and right to the base of 'the Hourglass,' a narrow rock/snow constriction that is the technical crux of the approach to the summit block (Class 3 scrambling, or a steep 35-45° snow climb in early season requiring an axe and solid self-arrest skills — watch for a moat opening at its base as the snow recedes). Above the Hourglass, continue on scree or snow toward the summit ridge and watch closely for a cairned, easy-to-miss notch on the right (climbers describe it as a 'dwarf door' — nearly invisible until you're directly in front of it); this notch is the route-finding key to the final gully leading to the true south summit, the last roughly 200 vertical feet of which is Class 4 with real exposure. Water is reliable at Lena Lake and along Lena Creek up to high camp; above camp, plan on snowmelt or carrying water, as there's nothing reliable once you're on the scree/couloir.

text: From the terraces near 5,500 ft (a possible bivy), head roughly north over ground that is occasionally fourth class, aiming for the notch in the South Brother's southeast ridge at about 6,100 ft.
runs: the notch in the south brother's southeast ridge

text: The roped traverse starts below the North Brother: scramble down easy rock to a flat spot to rope up, then belay a pitch of moderate snow on the east side of the ridge, protected with pickets and rock gear.
runs: of moderate snow on the east side of the ridge

text:
The arrival test is a step in the ridge crest at about 6,100 ft, and the way you know it is the right one is the thing that happens if you go 100 ft higher. Working up and rightward from camp on scree, heather and lumpy basalt, crossing many small ribs and gullies, you meet the crest. There are two places you can meet it. The higher one, at about 6,200 ft, is a small notch whose far side is a 200-foot cliff — a party that tops out there has to back off and traverse out on exposed ledges with Class 3-4 slots between them. The one you want is the small step in the crest at about 6,100 ft, from which the ground drops steeply but climbably into the snow-filled Great Basin.

So the fog test is: top out, then look down. If the far side goes, you are at the step and on route. If the far side is a cliff, you are a hundred feet too high — do not try to force it, come back down and traverse.

Second test, once in the Great Basin: from it you climb a moderately steep snow couloir angling toward the North Brother, narrowing to a snow finger that reaches the summit ridge. If your couloir is running away from the north summit rather than toward it, you crossed the basin in the wrong direction.

What the traverse itself feels like, so nobody mistakes the connecting ridge for a mistake: the crest between the two Brothers is giant boulders forming a jagged run of horns and pinnacles, and traversing it is slow. Slow is correct here. The route is roughly seven roped pitches — fourth class to the notch, steep snow into the Great Basin, moderate snow on the east ridge, a sparsely protected rock traverse on the west side, mixed ground with moat belays, and a final steep couloir to the South Brother.
runs: on scree heather and lumpy basalt crossing many small ribs and gullies

text: Starts on the north side of the tower, about 50 feet below the notch, at two semi-parallel diagonal cracks that form the crux. After the diagonals, the route follows a flake past a dead tree to a belay tree (reportedly deteriorating — back it up with gear). Pitch 2 traverses left beneath an overhang to a corner, then continues about 20 feet to the mouth of a cave, which is climbed through (~20 feet) to a belay on the far side. Pitch 3 climbs an easier crack and face to a tree belay at the summit.
runs: the notch at two semi parallel diagonal cracks

text: Traverse left beneath an overhang and around a corner to the mouth of 'the cave' (sling belay), then move through the cave itself — roughly 20 ft of traversing/squeezing — to a second belay at the far end. Bring a few extender slings or rope drag becomes a serious problem through this section.
runs: bring a few extender slings or rope drag

text: Begins on the right side of the South Face and follows flakes, corners, and splitters up to a broad ledge roughly halfway up the face. From the ledge, walk leftward to start the upper half of the climb; the first pitch above the ledge heads up to the left side of the most prominent arete/pillar in the middle of the upper face. After two more pitches, the route trends rightward and reaches the summit via blocky ground just right of a prominent chimney.
runs: on the right side of the south face
the first pitch above the ledge heads up to the left side of the most prominent arete/pillar

text:
The wall is clean white granite and it is visibly paler than what surrounds it, which is the first check that you are under the right formation. Follow the creek to the meadows and then up to the foot of it.

This route is the right-hand line. Start on the right side of the south face, on flakes, corners and splitters. Its neighbour begins with a layback off a large clean flake into a long left-facing corner system; if that is what is above you, walk right.

The defining feature is a broad ledge at half height, and it is the strongest thing this route has. Roughly halfway up the face the climbing arrives at a wide ledge that runs across the wall. That ledge is the route's hinge: from it you walk leftward before starting the upper half. A route that reaches a broad crossing ledge and then requires you to walk left along it is this one.

Confirm on the upper face. The first pitch above the ledge heads for the left side of the most prominent arete or pillar in the middle of the upper wall. That arete is the biggest feature up there and being on its left is the check. Two more pitches, then the line trends rightward to the summit.

The summit pitch separates the two routes absolutely. This one finishes on blocky ground just right of a prominent chimney. It does not go into the chimney. The neighbouring route tops out through a deep summit chimney. So: blocky ground beside a slot means this route; stemming up inside the slot means you have crossed onto the other line.

Negative marker lower down, since the two lines are close: if there was no broad crossing ledge and instead you moved rightward under a roof into a splitter to reach a smaller ledge, you are on the neighbour.

No descent has been described for this line itself. Because it shares the summit and the mid-face ledge with its neighbour, parties use that route's rappels down the south-east side: a seventy-metre rope, sparse fixed anchors, and enough webbing to build your own. Go up prepared to make anchors.
runs: on the right side of the south face

text: Single set of cams to #2 Camalot size, small-medium stoppers; double slings useful for the traverse and loose terrain.
runs: single set of cams to 2 camalot size small

text: About 1,000 ft of steep slabs lead to a small bivy ledge at the base of the near-vertical, 1,500-ft upper headwall. This sets up an early start on the crux the next day.

text: The documented crux: the FA account describes surmounting the 'final overhangs' on this pitch with the leader unable to see where the next piece of protection would be. First climbed with a short aid section (recorded as 5.9+ A2-), later free ascents rate it around 5.11-; treat the X rating as literal on a route this remote.
runs: see where the next piece of protection would be
